name: Zinza
confidence_why: Odom's SIL grammar sketch (2016) and the Zinza Orthography Statement (Odom 2015), in line with Odden's (2000) tonal analysis quoted there, describe Zinza as a language with lexical and grammatical tone, one high tone per word and tonal minimal pairs, and never mention stress; the only contrary statement, Seidel's 1898 sketch compiled from Lieutenant Kollmann's notes, which puts the 'Wortton' usually on the penultimate syllable, is an older second-hand impression that most plausibly records where the high tone was heard (it cannot fall on a word-final syllable), and Rehse's 1912-14 remark that accent in Haya-Zinza follows grammatical form fits grammatical tone rather than stress.
catalog_citation: Odom, Shannon Ronit. 2016. The Grammar Basics of Zinza. Dallas, Texas: SIL International (Uganda-Tanzania Branch, Language and Culture Archives). 26 pp. [Supporting: Odom, Shannon Ronit (based on previous work by Thomas G. Matthews and Dorien Kamphuis). 2015. Zinza Orthography Statement, Approved Orthography Edition, Final Edition October 2015. SIL International, Uganda-Tanzania Branch. 41 pp.]
catalog_locator: Odom 2016 pp. 2-3 ('A note about the Zinza Orthography' incl. footnote 2); Odom 2015 sec. 2.3 'Tone' pp. 8-10.
catalog_quote: Note that all five vowel phonemes have long vowel counterparts. There is both contrastive and conditioned vowel length, and both are written. [p. 2] Surface tone is written using the acute accent mark. Vowels can be marked for either high, rising, or falling tone.2 Low tones are not marked. Graphemes for each type of tone are shown below using a as the example vowel. Note that underlying tones of affixes are not marked throughout this document, since the relevant level of tone marking for orthography purposes is word-level surface tone. Tone: á [ɑ́], aá [ɑ̌ː], áa [ɑ̂ː] See the Zinza Orthography Statement (Odom 2015) for more information. [fn. 2] In Odden’s (2000) description of Zinza tonology, on long vowels he transcribes only level high tones and falling tones: “In penultimate long H-toned syllables, there are two contrasting tone patterns, namely a falling tone … and a level ~ rising tone …” (46). Based on native speaker perception of tone patterns on long vowels, these tones are transcribed in the orthography as rising or falling, not level or falling. [p. 3]

new_statements.quote: Die Betonung hängt im Ruziba nicht von der Anzahl der Silben eines Wortes oder von der Art der Bestandteile der Silbe ab, sondern lediglich von der grammatikalischen Form, in welcher das Wort oder der Satz stehen. [...] Diese Art und Weise der Betonung erschwert das Verstehen der Sprache sehr. Eine bestimmte Regel läßt sich auch für die Betonung noch nicht angeben. (ZfK 3: 4) — Die Bazinza haben keine eigene Sprache. Sie sprechen einen Dialekt des Ruziba, der hier Ruzinza heißt [...]. Die Abweichungen von dieser Grammatik sind so unbedeutend, daß man sie in Kürze in folgenden Punkten zusammenfassen kann. (ZfK 4: 257)
new_statements.translation: Accentuation in Ruziba does not depend on the number of syllables of a word or on the nature of the syllable's constituents, but solely on the grammatical form in which the word or the sentence stands. [...] This manner of accentuation makes understanding the language very difficult. No definite rule can yet be given for the accentuation either. — The Bazinza have no language of their own. They speak a dialect of Ruziba, here called Ruzinza [...]. The deviations from this grammar are so insignificant that they can be summarised briefly in the following points.
new_statements.citation: Rehse, Hermann. 1912/13. Die Sprache der Baziba in Deutsch-Ostafrika. Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen 3(1): 1-33, §4 Betonung, p. 4; applied to Zinza by Rehse, Hermann. 1914. Eigentümlichkeiten in der Sprache der Bazinza in Deutsch-Ostafrika. Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen 4: 257.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Rehse, word accent (what he writes as an acute 'Ton') is not positional (not tied to syllable count, weight or the penult) but is determined by the grammatical form of the word; he can state no general rule, only special cases: the augment/'article' is accented (ómukazi, ómushaija), the stem syllable of underived infinitives (kutéra, kubóna), some verbal derivatives accent the stem and others the penult (kugámba vs kugambíra), and subject pronouns are accented (yámutera). Given that Haya and Zinza are tone languages (Odden 2000 'phrasal tonology'), this 'Betonung' is most plausibly grammatical tone, not stress; the source itself never says 'tone language'. Statement is for Ruziba (Haya); Rehse 1914 applies the grammar wholesale to Ruzinza.
new_statements.exceptions: Rehse says no rule can be stated and only special cases can be listed: article/augment accented; infinitive stem syllable; derivatives vary between stem and penult; subject pronouns accented; the acute marks the accented syllable throughout the grammar. Preface also mentions 'die verschiedenartige Betonung eines und desselben Wortes' and 'das fast völlige Fehlen eines Satz-Akzentes' (p. 1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word and sentence ('in welcher das Wort oder der Satz stehen'); 1912 field notes by a colonial administrator, impressionistic, no instrumental basis; the question is marked by intonation only (p. 6).
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand accent statement that could be opened is Rehse's 1912/13 grammar of Ruziba (= Haya, haya1250; Kiziba dialect), not of Zinza. Rehse's 1914 Zinza note (ZfK 4: 257) states that the Bazinza "have no language of their own" but speak a dialect of Ruziba called Ruzinza whose deviations from that grammar are "so insignificant" that he lists them in a few points, none concerning accent; so the Ruziba statement applies to Zinza only by Rehse's own equation of the two. Glottolog separates zinz1238 from haya1250, and Odden (2000, 2006) treats Zinza as a language in its own right with its own phrasal tonology.

new_statements.relation_note: Language not in the catalog; the only existing statement is Rehse's 1912/13 Ruziba (Haya) 'Betonung' paragraph applied to Zinza by Rehse 1914. Odom describes Zinza itself as a lexical-and-grammatical tone language with vowel length and says nothing about stress, so it neither confirms nor contradicts Rehse's grammatically conditioned 'Ton'; it refines the record by fixing the prosodic type (tone + length) for Zinza proper and confirms an earlier compilation note ('tone only, no stress statement').
new_statements.rule_in_words: The sketch is morphosyntax only (noun classes, agreement, TAM, extensions, dependent clauses). Its only prosodic content is the orthography note: Zinza has contrastive and conditioned vowel length and a word-level surface tone system (H, rising, falling on long vowels; L unmarked), with a footnote citing Odden 2000 on tone patterns of penultimate long H-toned syllables. The words stress, accent (other than 'acute accent mark') and prominence do not occur anywhere in the 26 pages; no statement of stress placement or of its absence.
new_statements.identity_note: Odom 2016 describes Zinza proper (JE23, ISO zin; Geita and Mwanza Regions, southwestern Lake Victoria), written in the current SIL orthography; data checked with Zinza speakers (Kabika Juvenari, Mussa Ipimilo). The existing Rehse statement is about Ruziba (Kiziba Haya, haya1250) and reaches Zinza only through Rehse's own equation of the two. Seidel 1898 'Usindja' = the Zinza area (Usinja), not opened.

new_statements.quote: 3. Der Wortton ruht gewöhnlich auf der vorletzten Silbe. Abweichungen hiervon sind durch den Acut (á) gekennzeichnet. Treten Wortbildungs- oder Flexionssilben an ein Wort, so ändert sich der Regel nach die Betonung, eine Ausnahme macht indessen die Endung des Perfekts (vergl. § 44 f.). [p.152] ... m) Der Wortton zeigt die vorherrschende Neigung, auf der vorletzten Silbe zu ruhen, z. B. yawatéra, akagúla, kulemíla. [p.153] ... [Die Vokale] werden wie im Deutschen ausgesprochen, und zwar lang in betonter Silbe, sonst kurz. [p.151]
new_statements.translation: 3. The word accent usually rests on the penultimate syllable. Deviations from this are marked with the acute (á). When derivational or inflectional syllables are added to a word, the accent as a rule shifts; the ending of the perfect, however, is an exception (cf. § 44 f). ... m) The word accent shows the prevailing tendency to rest on the penultimate syllable, e.g. yawatéra, akagúla, kulemíla. ... [The vowels] are pronounced as in German, long in a stressed syllable, otherwise short.

new_statements.relation_note: Language not in catalog. The only existing statement (Rehse 1912/13, §4 p.4, on Ruziba = Haya, extended to Zinza by Rehse 1914) says accent depends only on grammatical form, not on syllable count, i.e. no positional rule ('unclear or contradictory'). Seidel/Kollmann 1898, describing Ki-Sindja proper (Usindja north to Usui, between Emin Pasha Gulf and Smith Sound, SW Lake Victoria = Zinza), give a definite positional rule: usually penultimate, with marked exceptions. Different type of statement (fixed penult vs. morphologically determined/unclear); note Rehse's rule is for a different variety (Haya). Modern sources already held by the project (Odom 2016, SIL orthography statement, Odden 2000…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent ('Wortton') normally on the penultimate syllable of the word; it moves with the word edge when suffixes/formatives are added (so it stays penultimate), except that the perfect ending (-ile, §44f) does not attract the shift; lexical deviations exist and are marked with an acute in the transcription; the stressed vowel is pronounced long, unstressed vowels short. No description of tone (only p.167: the preposition omu forms one 'Toneinheit' with the following word; p.166: na + vowel merge into one stressed long vowel).
new_statements.exceptions: 'gewöhnlich' (usually) penultimate; deviations marked by acute accent in the texts; accent shifts when word-formation or inflectional syllables are added, but the perfect ending (§44 f, -ile) is an exception to the shift.
new_statements.identity_note: Seidel 1898 describes 'Ki-Sindja', 'Sprache der Eingeborenen von Usindja', spoken 'in Usindja nördlich bis Usui; in dem Land zwischen Emin Pascha Golf und Smith Golf' (SW shore of Lake Victoria), recorded by Pr.-Lt. Kollmann, station chief of Mwanza (p.171 notes) = Zinza (zinz1238); he notes the resident Wahuma there speak Kihuma instead. The scan read is the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek copy 390622-C.4.1898 (barcode +Z319298805, digitized with Google 2026-02-11), i.e. the same scan as the listed Google Books volume CXxNJTruxGgC, whose Google endpoints remain could not be reached by automated download.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction, but the two kinds of source describe different things. Rehse 1912/13 (the only existing statement, written for Ruziba = Haya and transferred to Zinza by Rehse's 1914 remark that Ruzinza is a dialect of Ruziba) says 'Betonung' depends solely on grammatical form and no rule can be given; Odom 2016 (Zinza proper, SIL, with the 2015 Zinza Orthography Statement it refers to) describes a lexical-and-grammatical tone system with contrastive vowel length and never mentions stress or accent. Rehse's grammatically conditioned 'Ton' is most naturally read as the grammatical tone Odom describes, not as word stress, so the sources are compatible; the catalog should not carry a stress placement for Zinza on Rehse's authority. Seidel 1898 could not be opened and may say something else. Seidel 1898 (from Kollmann's Zinza notes) states that word accent usually falls on the penultimate syllable, shifting with added suffixes (except the perfect ending) and with lexical deviations marked by an acute. The previously found statement, Rehse 1912/13 §4 (written for Ruziba/Haya and carried over to Zinza by Rehse 1914, who calls Zinza a dialect of Ruziba), says accent depends only on the grammatical form and not on syllable count, giving no positional rule. These disagree in type (positional penult vs. grammatically determined); Rehse's is about a neighbouring variety (Haya), Seidel's about Ki-Sindja proper.
